findings.title: Async legacy writes are canceled with the request
findings.body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s) derived from the incoming request context. WithTimeoutCause is canceled as soon as the parent is canceled, which the apiserver does as soon as the handler returns—immediately after this goroutine is spawned. The 10s timeout therefore never applies, and the legacy write is aborted with context.Canceled on almost every request. Mode 3's rollback/safety copy to legacy does not actually persist, so a later read from legacy or a rollback from unified storage drops creates, updates, and deletes that clients were already told succeeded. Derive the background work from context.WithoutCancel (or Background plus copied values) and then apply the timeout. The same pattern is at the Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163) goroutines.

findings.title: Legacy update re-applies the request instead of the unified result
findings.body: Update used to materialize one updated object from unified storage and pass that exact object to both stores (via updateWrapper). It now calls Legacy.Update with the original objInfo after Storage.Update returns. Legacy storage will Get its own copy and run UpdatedObject/Preconditions again. In mode 3, clients read resourceVersion from unified storage, so those preconditions do not match legacy's resourceVersion and the legacy update fails with a conflict (or, if preconditions are absent, applies the transform to a divergent legacy object). Patch goes through this same Update path. The legacy "safe measure" copy therefore does not match what was committed to unified storage. Write the object returned by Storage.Update (and clear legacy resourceVersion preconditions) rather than re-running objInfo.

findings.title: Async legacy Create races on the caller's object
findings.body: After Storage.Create returns, the goroutine calls Legacy.Create with the same obj pointer the caller still holds. Storage implementations commonly mutate that object in place and return it as created, and the apiserver then encodes created while Legacy.Create is still mutating resourceVersion, UID, timestamps, or unstructured maps. That is a data race: responses can be corrupted or the process can panic, and the legacy row can be written from a half-updated object. Deep-copy the object (and any options the legacy call mutates) before handing it to the goroutine. The same sharing applies to objInfo on the async Update path (line 139), which is not safe to use again after Storage.Update has consumed it.

findings.title: Storage failures and legacy latency are recorded on the wrong metric
findings.body: On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) with the storage start time, and on Storage.Update failure it does the same (line 129). Those paths never touched legacy, so unified-storage errors disappear from the storage metric and show up as legacy failures. DeleteCollection's async legacy call then does the opposite: line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for Legacy.DeleteCollection, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors inflate the storage series and never appear on the legacy series. Success paths for Create/Update correctly use recordStorageDuration, which shows these error-path calls are swapped. Dashboards and alerts for mode 3 will page on the wrong store and hide the safety-write failures.

findings.title: Successful Delete records the object name as the kind label
findings.body: The success path of Delete calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the kind label, while the error path on line 103 and every other method pass options.Kind. Every distinct deleted name becomes a new Prometheus label value. That blows up cardinality on the storage-duration metric and makes delete latency unusable for dashboards. Pass options.Kind, consistent with the error path.

findings.title: Legacy write errors are dropped with no log
findings.body: The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection failures. The goroutines now only feed a duration metric and discard errObjectSt (Create line 56, Update line 140, Delete line 113, DeleteCollection line 166). Combined with the mis-attributed metrics, a legacy timeout, conflict, or outage leaves unified storage and legacy permanently diverged with nothing in the logs identifying the object or the error. Log the legacy error (with name/kind) before recording the metric. Also, Delete puts d.Log into the context on line 97 instead of the enriched log, so even storage-side logs for that method lack name, kind, and method.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
findings.body: Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately, but Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection fire unbounded goroutines that can still be inside Legacy.* for up to 10 seconds. Shutdown therefore either drops the safety write or calls into a store that has already been destroyed (use-after-close, errors, or panics). There is also no limit on how many of these goroutines can pile up under write load. Track in-flight legacy work and wait for it in Destroy (or cancel it explicitly), and bound concurrency.

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests do not match async dual-write behavior
findings.body: The Create failure case only stubs Legacy.Create and never stubs Storage.Create, but mode 3 fails the request only when unified storage fails, so this case does not exercise the error path (and, with an unconfigured mock returning a nil error, assert.Error fails). Success cases stub legacy but return as soon as Storage.* returns, with no wait and no AssertExpectations, so they pass even if the legacy goroutine never runs. The goroutine can also call the shared testify mock after t.Run returns, which races and can panic. None of the tests cover legacy failure, timeout, or the requirement that legacy receives the object unified storage actually stored. Synchronize the goroutine (or inject a synchronous hook) and assert both stores.

findings.title: Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated synchronously
findings.body: The new file/unified/etcd mode 3 subtests call doPlaylistTests, whose k8s CRUD case immediately lists and gets the same playlists through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (and getFromBothAPIs does the same after update and delete). Mode 3 returns as soon as unified storage succeeds and only then writes legacy in a goroutine that is also tied to the request context. Those assertions will fail or flake whenever the legacy copy has not landed yet, and they will fail consistently if the request context cancels the legacy write. The new mode 3 cases need to wait until the legacy copy is visible, or the test will not actually prove the safety write.
